subtitle: From Genomic Computation to Adaptive Machine Intelligence
entryAssumptions: Ability to follow a logical explanation
Completion of Book I to its eventually verified exit contract; not satisfied by its existing two-chapter draft

chapters.part: I · From a familiar genome to a new question
chapters.title: Programs, genomes and the question of Evolutor
chapters.readerQuestion: Why compare a genome with a program?
frames: Show a fixed program reacting to two inputs
Recall one genome with different expression states
Place a question mark, not an equals sign, between biology and software
chapters.mathBridge: No tuple or cost formula. Explain program as written instructions; model and neural network are destinations taught in Chapter 3 and Chapter 7.
chapters.codeLab: Paper comparison of what is stored, what changes and what is observed; no new code.
chapters.exercise: Recognize an analogy; identify a missing mechanism; explain that ordinary software can also respond and change.

chapters.part: I · From a familiar genome to a new question
chapters.title: Programs that choose and remember
chapters.readerQuestion: How can the same input produce a different answer after a different history?
frames: Run the same input after two histories
Separate stored instructions from changing state
chapters.mathBridge: Replay addition and assignment before a state-update table; no recurrence symbols yet.
chapters.codeLab: Refresh Book I Python functions, dictionaries and tests, then build a two-command stateful program.
chapters.exercise: Trace both histories; test a reset; distinguish the current input, remembered state and stored instructions.

chapters.part: I · From a familiar genome to a new question
chapters.title: Machine learning with one tiny model
chapters.readerQuestion: How can examples help set a rule's adjustable numbers?
frames: Place measured points on a small chart
Try a rule with one adjustable multiplier
Freeze the numbers for a new input
chapters.mathBridge: Explain input, weight and offset using prices before y=wx+b; errors before mean squared loss. Training uses manual trials, not gradients.
chapters.codeLab: Plain Python predictions and a short table of trial parameter choices; keep training and inference functions separate.
chapters.exercise: Compute one prediction; compare two trial settings; distinguish fitting examples from success on new ones.

chapters.part: I · From a familiar genome to a new question
chapters.title: Data, uncertainty and fair evaluation
chapters.readerQuestion: Why can a model look good and still fail on new examples?
frames: Sort examples into three named boxes
Repeat with a different random seed
chapters.mathBridge: Recall Book I probabilities; concrete spreads precede variance, sampling uncertainty and interval notation; teach what an interval does not guarantee.
chapters.codeLab: Create a tiny split with duplicate detection; keep an untouched test file.
chapters.exercise: Identify leakage; compute a mean error; explain why one run is insufficient evidence.

chapters.part: II · Learning the language of neural models
chapters.title: Vectors, matrices and tensors as data containers
chapters.readerQuestion: How can one rule process several measurements together?
frames: Add a batch axis with labeled dimensions
chapters.mathBridge: Recall Book I dot products and matrix multiplication explicitly; every axis gets a name before tensor notation.
chapters.codeLab: Plain Python arrays with shape labels and a paper tensor-layout exercise; PyTorch tensor construction and setup wait for Chapter 8.
chapters.exercise: Compute a tiny product; label axes; diagnose an accidental broadcast.

chapters.part: II · Learning the language of neural models
chapters.title: Slopes, gradients and improving a prediction
chapters.readerQuestion: Which small change would reduce the error?
frames: Move one parameter slightly left and right
chapters.mathBridge: Finite differences and rise-over-run precede derivatives; one variable before partial derivatives; chain rule before gradient update notation.
chapters.codeLab: Calculate a finite-difference gradient in plain Python and compare a hand-derived scalar gradient.
chapters.exercise: Compute a slope; show an overly large step; explain local improvement versus a global guarantee.

chapters.part: II · Learning the language of neural models
chapters.title: Neural networks built one layer at a time
chapters.readerQuestion: Why put simple transformations in layers?
chapters.mathBridge: Teach linear versus nonlinear with pictures before matrix-layer notation; convolution is a local shared-weight operation before the acronym convolutional neural network.
chapters.codeLab: Tiny scalar network first, then batched matrix forward pass; no large architecture.
chapters.exercise: Compute two neurons; compare linear compositions and nonlinear layers; trace one gradient path.

chapters.part: II · Learning the language of neural models
chapters.title: A complete small training loop in PyTorch
chapters.readerQuestion: What changes during training, and what stays fixed during inference?
frames: Repeat, then freeze parameters and predict
chapters.mathBridge: Map each code operation to Chapter 6 arithmetic; explain gradient accumulation and reset before optimizer calls.
chapters.codeLab: Teach installation, tensors, autograd, zero_grad, backward and step; separate no-update inference and evaluation behavior.
chapters.exercise: Repair a missing gradient reset; reproduce a tiny run; verify parameters are unchanged by inference.

chapters.part: III · Sequences and memory
chapters.title: Tokens, embeddings and predicting the next symbol
chapters.readerQuestion: How do written symbols become numbers a model can use?
frames: Split a tiny sequence using a declared tokenizer
chapters.mathBridge: Explain categorical probabilities and normalized positive scores before softmax; logarithm recall precedes cross-entropy; IDs are not numeric distances.
chapters.codeLab: Build a tiny tokenizer and embedding lookup, then a next-token table baseline.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish a character from a token; compute a tiny normalized distribution; prevent future-token leakage.

chapters.part: III · Sequences and memory
chapters.title: Recurrence: remembering one step at a time
chapters.readerQuestion: How can a model carry something from the previous symbol?
frames: Retain part of old state and add new input
Read a second symbol with changed state
Unroll the same update across time
chapters.mathBridge: Old amount minus lost amount plus new amount precedes (1-d)x+pu; label before/after state, then generalize to RNN notation.
chapters.codeLab: Exact rational leaky example before a small trained RNN; distinguish hand-set recurrence from learning.
chapters.exercise: Compute two steps; compare histories; test reset boundaries and explain why memory is not yet learning.

chapters.part: III · Sequences and memory
chapters.title: Gates and state-space models
chapters.readerQuestion: What should a compact state keep or forget?
frames: Compare a GRU update with fixed retention
Draw state transition and observation separately
chapters.mathBridge: Matrix recurrence follows scalar recurrence; introduce eigenvalue intuition only if used, with a two-dimensional example; no unprepared stability theorem.
chapters.codeLab: Implement a small GRU and a declared linear SSM baseline before contemporary variants.
chapters.exercise: Trace a gate at zero and one; compare state sizes; state what information a compact state may lose.

chapters.part: III · Sequences and memory
chapters.title: Attention as a weighted lookup
chapters.readerQuestion: Which earlier symbol should matter now?
frames: Give three tokens labeled information cards
chapters.mathBridge: Use explicit two-number vectors, dot products, softmax and weighted sum before QK-transpose notation.
chapters.codeLab: Hand-compute a three-token example, then plain tensors and autograd parity checks.
chapters.exercise: Compute weights; explain query/key/value roles; demonstrate a causal-mask failure.

chapters.part: III · Sequences and memory
chapters.title: From one attention head to a Transformer
chapters.readerQuestion: How do small attention operations form a useful model?
chapters.mathBridge: Teach mean/variance normalization and skip addition before block equations; every tensor shape remains labeled.
chapters.codeLab: Build one small causal block and test shape, masking and checkpoint reload before stacking.
chapters.exercise: Trace one token through a block; explain why position matters; reject a full architecture diagram with unlabeled axes.

chapters.part: III · Sequences and memory
chapters.title: Caches, retrieval and external memory
chapters.readerQuestion: Why keep earlier work, and when should a system look something up?
frames: Generate the next token reusing them
Compare lookup in an external document collection
chapters.mathBridge: Count stored rows and reused operations before memory formulas; cache stores computations, not a magical source of factual truth.
chapters.codeLab: Compare cached and uncached tiny-model outputs; build a tiny exact retrieval index.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish recurrent state, KV cache and retrieved documents; test stale-cache and mismatched-history cases.

chapters.part: IV · Existing software before genomic abstractions
chapters.title: If/else, dispatch, plugins and dynamic routing
chapters.readerQuestion: What already selects only part of a program?
frames: Choose a function by a name
Compare a scan with an indexed lookup
Record selection work separately from execution work
chapters.mathBridge: Count concrete comparisons before cost tuples; prove equivalence only after tracing matching inputs and assumptions.
chapters.codeLab: Rebuild the old dispatch example with explicit errors, purity assumptions and counted events.
chapters.exercise: Find a duplicate-name bug; compare costs honestly; explain why selective execution alone is not novel.

chapters.part: IV · Existing software before genomic abstractions
chapters.title: Mixture of experts and learned routing
chapters.readerQuestion: Can the choice of a module itself be learned?
frames: Show an overloaded expert and balancing response
chapters.mathBridge: Top-k selection and weighted sums precede routing loss; distinguish stored and activated parameters.
chapters.codeLab: Implement a tiny routed baseline with a matched dense control; report routing cost as well as expert work.
chapters.exercise: Trace a route; identify collapse; distinguish sparsity from an established end-to-end speedup.

chapters.part: IV · Existing software before genomic abstractions
chapters.title: Source code, compilers, runtimes and interfaces
chapters.readerQuestion: What happens between writing a program and running it?
frames: Call a library through a named interface
Compare separate processes and threads sharing memory
chapters.mathBridge: No compiler-theory prerequisites; distinguish representation from running instance before any formal semantics.
chapters.codeLab: Build a tiny expression interpreter before optional compilation; document an API with inputs and failure outputs.
chapters.exercise: Match objects to stages; distinguish process from thread; explain interpreter and runtime without treating them as synonyms.

chapters.part: IV · Existing software before genomic abstractions
chapters.title: Services, databases, protocols and scheduling
chapters.readerQuestion: Why does serving several requests need more than a model?
frames: Send a request to a service
Fetch a row from a database
chapters.mathBridge: Time a single request before latency; count completed requests per interval before throughput; teach query operator order before planning costs.
chapters.codeLab: Single-process simulated service and queue; no production deployment required.
chapters.exercise: Trace request identity; compare batching tradeoffs; distinguish a cache from an authoritative database.

chapters.part: IV · Existing software before genomic abstractions
chapters.title: Baselines, oracles and resource-matched experiments
chapters.readerQuestion: What would count as a fair improvement?
frames: Specify a task before choosing a model
Put simple and advanced baselines alongside a proposal
chapters.mathBridge: Report sample counts, distributions and uncertainty before summary rankings; separate parameters, executed work and wall time.
chapters.codeLab: Shared experiment contract for Markov, MLP, CNN, GRU, Transformer and SSM baselines; teach Markov assumption with a small transition table here.
chapters.exercise: Design a falsifier; expose answer leakage; explain why an oracle checks a task but does not certify intelligence.

chapters.part: V · Borrowing from biology carefully
chapters.title: Regulation, expression and different timescales
chapters.readerQuestion: What changes within a cell, and what changes across generations?
frames: Add a separately typed control relation
Hold DNA fixed while state changes
chapters.mathBridge: Recall Book I units and recurrence; a biological cartoon is not a fitted differential equation.
chapters.codeLab: Revisit a toy control example next to an ordinary stateful software baseline.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish control from sequence reversal; classify state change, gene expression and inherited change.

chapters.part: V · Borrowing from biology carefully
chapters.title: Analogies that can fail
chapters.readerQuestion: What remains after comparing a biological idea with existing software?
frames: Pair gene with module using a question-mark link
Cross out an equivalence when mechanisms differ
chapters.mathBridge: No formalism yet; specify observable differences and excluded biological features in ordinary language.
chapters.codeLab: Write a mechanism contract and a nearest-baseline checklist before any genomic class.
chapters.exercise: Reject a renamed existing mechanism; propose a discriminating experiment; leave an unsupported claim open.

chapters.part: V · Borrowing from biology carefully
chapters.title: Learning parameters and changing structure
chapters.readerQuestion: How does changing a number differ from changing a program?
chapters.mathBridge: Teach tree and syntax node with an arithmetic expression before genetic-programming notation; introduce search spaces concretely.
chapters.codeLab: Compare parameter fitting, pruning and small program search under a declared budget.
chapters.exercise: Classify changes; track who evaluates candidates; identify evaluation-set reuse and selection bias.

chapters.part: V · Borrowing from biology carefully
chapters.title: Development as building a representation
chapters.readerQuestion: Can a compact description construct a larger program?
chapters.mathBridge: Explain grammar, node type and validation locally before formal grammar notation; no equivalence with embryology.
chapters.codeLab: Build a tiny checked expression plan from a declarative source.
chapters.exercise: Find an invalid type; distinguish expansion from learning; identify the biological details intentionally absent.

chapters.part: V · Borrowing from biology carefully
chapters.title: A minimal genomic-computation hypothesis
chapters.readerQuestion: What precise system are we proposing to test?
frames: Recall stored modules, context and state
Execute it with an explicit trace
Show an optional separately authorized structural proposal
chapters.mathBridge: Only now collect already taught components into a tuple; explain transition rules and costs one at a time.
chapters.codeLab: Specify a small deterministic reference before neural implementations; all novelty claims remain hypotheses.
chapters.exercise: Derive one transition; exhibit nearest-baseline equivalence; write a condition that would falsify the additional mechanism.

chapters.part: VI · Implementing only what is specified
chapters.title: Classes, interfaces and a UML model
chapters.readerQuestion: How can the software structure express the proposed rules?
frames: Compare a blueprint class with two instances
Teach class compartments and relationship symbols
Draw Genome, Gene and Regulator classes
chapters.mathBridge: No unexplained engineering notation; cardinalities are illustrated with concrete object counts first.
chapters.codeLab: Reference classes follow the Chapter 24 contract; class diagram names must match code.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish class from instance; repair an ownership edge; test interface preconditions.

chapters.part: VI · Implementing only what is specified
chapters.title: From a request to an expression trace
chapters.readerQuestion: Who talks to whom during one request?
frames: Send context from Runtime to Regulator
chapters.mathBridge: Time flows down, messages sideways; distinguish return from a fresh request before asynchronous detail.
chapters.codeLab: Single-request reference execution with deterministic trace IDs and explicit failures.
chapters.exercise: Trace one request; detect a backwards message; compare diagram events to recorded code events.

chapters.part: VI · Implementing only what is specified
chapters.title: Traces, credit and explanations
chapters.readerQuestion: Which component deserves credit, and what can a trace actually explain?
frames: Remove one component in a controlled run
Compare the result with the original
chapters.mathBridge: Event correlation before causal claims; gradients and interventions answer different questions.
chapters.codeLab: Trace-based ablation harness with a counterfactual baseline where well-defined.
chapters.exercise: Explain why a logged route is not a causal proof; identify missing provenance; propose a controlled intervention.

chapters.part: VI · Implementing only what is specified
chapters.title: Structural proposals and their lifecycle
chapters.readerQuestion: When may a proposed edit become active?
chapters.mathBridge: State diagrams precede transition tables; explain safety invariants with invalid examples.
chapters.codeLab: Pending, validated, tested, accepted and rejected states with illegal-transition tests.
chapters.exercise: Reject an untested transition; preserve the old version; distinguish bounded validation from universal correctness.

chapters.part: VI · Implementing only what is specified
chapters.title: Training a candidate Evolutor model
chapters.readerQuestion: Does the proposed mechanism help beyond the taught baselines?
frames: Separate parameter updates from structural proposals
chapters.mathBridge: Map each loss term to a measured objective before combining it; disclose update schedules and budgets.
chapters.codeLab: Small PyTorch candidate with identical evaluation interface to Chapter 19; no large-run result invented.
chapters.exercise: Audit a training loop; test frozen-structure behavior; report an inconclusive or negative outcome correctly.

chapters.part: VI · Implementing only what is specified
chapters.title: An inference runtime with clear boundaries
chapters.readerQuestion: Which parts must run for one prediction?
chapters.mathBridge: No new optimization formulas; teach contracts and observable behavior before implementation shortcuts.
chapters.codeLab: Reference runtime with backend adapter; inference must not silently train or accept structural edits.
chapters.exercise: Trace a component failure; test parameter immutability; compare class and component diagrams.

chapters.part: VII · Engineering and reproducibility
chapters.title: Model identity, formats and checkpoints
chapters.readerQuestion: How do we know which model produced this result?
chapters.mathBridge: Explain byte representation and hash purpose before digest notation; integrity is not authenticity.
chapters.codeLab: Round-trip serialization tests, schema validation and explicit incompatible-version errors.
chapters.exercise: Find a missing configuration field; distinguish matching filename from matching model; reject silent fallback.

chapters.part: VII · Engineering and reproducibility
chapters.title: Managing recurrent state, KV and external memory
chapters.readerQuestion: How can several requests share hardware without sharing private state?
frames: Assign two requests separate state slots
Verify the other history is unchanged
chapters.mathBridge: Labeled byte counts and page sizes precede capacity equations; distinguish logical history from physical location.
chapters.codeLab: Small memory-manager simulation with isolation, eviction and reset tests.
chapters.exercise: Detect cross-request leakage; calculate capacity; explain why recurrent state and KV have different contracts.

chapters.part: VII · Engineering and reproducibility
chapters.title: Batching, queues and latency
chapters.readerQuestion: Why can throughput improve while some users wait longer?
frames: Let completed requests leave while new ones enter
chapters.mathBridge: Teach percentile from sorted waiting times before p95; simple arrival examples before queueing formulas.
chapters.codeLab: Discrete-event serving simulator with declared arrival traces; no production performance claim.
chapters.exercise: Calculate waiting times; identify starvation; compare a throughput gain with tail-latency cost.

chapters.part: VII · Engineering and reproducibility
chapters.title: Parity, profiling and optimization
chapters.readerQuestion: How do we make it faster without changing what it computes?
frames: Locate measured work in a profile
chapters.mathBridge: Absolute and relative numerical tolerance precede parity thresholds; timing distribution precedes speedup ratios.
chapters.codeLab: Reference-versus-optimized harness with warm-up, synchronization and hardware/version records.
chapters.exercise: Reject unequal workloads; diagnose a tolerance failure; separate logical-event counts from elapsed time.

chapters.part: VII · Engineering and reproducibility
chapters.title: Serving, observability and safe rollback
chapters.readerQuestion: How do we observe and recover a running service?
frames: Observe logs and metrics without exposing secrets
chapters.mathBridge: Service goals and measured thresholds precede any availability formula; security is a separate review discipline.
chapters.codeLab: Local deployment diagram and failure-injection exercise; no live service or credentials required.
chapters.exercise: Distinguish authentication from authorization; trace rollback state; redact a sensitive log.

chapters.part: VIII · Evidence, failure and the frontier
chapters.title: Failed ideas as a source of knowledge
chapters.readerQuestion: What should we learn when the idea does not win?
frames: State a claim and its failure condition
chapters.mathBridge: Teach multiple comparisons and selection effects with repeated toy trials before significance language.
chapters.codeLab: Archive all declared runs, including crashes and null results; use synthetic records only when explicitly labeled.
chapters.exercise: Separate bug, underpowered test and refuted claim; write a transparent negative-result report.

chapters.part: VIII · Evidence, failure and the frontier
chapters.title: DNA sequence models: DOGMA and Hermon DNA as questions
chapters.readerQuestion: Which architectural distinction survives beyond a project name?
frames: Compare a Transformer DNA model with a non-Transformer model
Place DOGMA and Hermon DNA names only after source and artifact audit
chapters.mathBridge: Reuse established equations; no new family definition from branding and no claim of validated taxonomy.
chapters.codeLab: Re-audit source, dataset splits, checkpoints and licenses before experiments; runnable substitutes are clearly labeled.
chapters.exercise: Separate name, architecture and evidence; design a symmetry control; leave an unverifiable claim unresolved.

chapters.part: VIII · Evidence, failure and the frontier
chapters.title: Transfer, continual learning and populations
chapters.readerQuestion: Does an improvement survive a changed task?
frames: Continue learning and recheck the first
chapters.mathBridge: Teach task distributions through concrete examples; distinguish adaptation budget from zero-shot evaluation.
chapters.codeLab: Two-task forgetting study with frozen controls and explicit adaptation budgets.
chapters.exercise: Identify hidden retraining; compare retention and transfer; report costs of population search.

chapters.part: VIII · Evidence, failure and the frontier
chapters.title: AGI claims and an operational scorecard
chapters.readerQuestion: What does a narrow result allow us to say about general intelligence?
frames: Mark measured, failed and untested cells
Show unresolved safety and transfer boundaries
chapters.mathBridge: No single magic scalar; explain operational definition and uncertainty before any aggregate score.
chapters.codeLab: Generate a scorecard from actual experiment records; unknown cells stay unknown.
chapters.exercise: Reject a unit-test-to-AGI inference; propose disconfirming tests; state the limits of the chosen definition.

chapters.part: VIII · Evidence, failure and the frontier
chapters.title: Capstone: a reproducible research-engineering argument
chapters.readerQuestion: Can another reader reproduce both the result and the boundary of the claim?
frames: Connect mechanism to code and diagrams
chapters.mathBridge: Use only established tools; require every equation and plotted quantity to trace to a definition and artifact.
chapters.codeLab: Release a small reproducible package with source, UML, tests, records and limitations; publication and rights gates remain explicit.
chapters.exercise: Present the strongest bounded claim, a failed alternative and the next falsifying experiment.
